newsitem.title: CHINA: China central bank says would offset reserve cut.
newsitem.headline: China central bank says would offset reserve cut.

text.p: China's central bank is studying a possible cut in the bank reserve requirement but any reduction would be offset by a reduction in relending to commercial banks, a central bank spokesman said on Wednesday.
The current reserve ratio of 13 percent was set in 1988 and there were studies concerning a possible revision, bank spokesman Ma Delun told reporters.
One such proposal has been to cut the requirement to 10 percent of commercial bank deposits, the official media have reported.
Those funds are lent back to commercial banks in what the bank considers to be a reallocation of resources within the banking system and among the various regions in China, Ma said.
"If we reduce the 13 percent requirement to 10 percent we will recall relending by the central bank to commercial banks by an equal amount," he said.
Some economists have called for a reduction in the reserve requirement as a way of loosening credit.
They have said cash-strapped state enterprises were badly in need of interest rate relief.
China, emboldened by a sharp drop in inflation, has already cut interest rates twice this year.
Chinese central bankers, however, have tried to play down prospects for another interest rate cut in the near future.
They have also been eager to show that the cuts do not send a signal to the market that there would be a substantial easing of monetary policy.
The spokesman repeated previous bank statements, saying the central bank would maintain its "appropriately tight" monetary policy over the next five-year plan of 1996-2000.
The bank spokesman also said China's macro-economic controls had produced some degree of success and that key indicators, including money supply statistics, were approaching their target levels.
A rise in foreign exchange reserves this year was likely to have some impact on inflation, he said.
Bank officials have put the nation's foreign exchange reserves at about $96 billion as of the end of September.
They have said, however, that reserves were not a key contributor to domestic inflation.
